claims.text: The initial coating is elemental chromium deposited on zirconium-alloy cladding.
The proposed intervention is to add a small amount of aluminum to the chromium coating.
Aluminum added to the chromium coating will oxidize during high-temperature exposure to form Al2O3.
The resulting alumina will form a stable, thin, continuous layer within or at the coating–substrate interface.
The alumina layer will act as a diffusion barrier.
The proposed diffusion barrier will reduce Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion compromises the integrity of elemental chromium coatings.
The aluminum-modified chromium coating will maintain oxidation resistance in approximately 300°C PWR primary water.
The aluminum-modified chromium coating will maintain oxidation resistance in accident-relevant steam at approximately 1000–1200°C.
Relative to elemental chromium, the aluminum-modified coating will exhibit less cracking or peeling.
Relative to elemental chromium, the aluminum-modified coating will exhibit reduced interfacial transport of chromium and zirconium.
Elemental chromium coatings provide good oxidation resistance before interdiffusion-induced failure occurs.
Keeping the aluminum content low enough will avoid significant phase changes in the chromium coating.
The intervention is applicable to long-duration exposure in approximately 300°C PWR water.
The intervention is applicable to transient steam exposure up to approximately 1200°C.
The optimum aluminum content and reproducibility of continuous alumina-layer formation have not yet been established.
Long-term neutron irradiation may affect the stability of the proposed alumina barrier, but this behavior is undetermined.
